first.rationale: Triage logic: I verified the two beliefs that are both most consequential to this week's single slot and most weakly supported for the stated objective (sustainable long-term qualified revenue). (1) memory_86 underwrites my intended action directly, and its recorded evidence is proxy-metric only \u2014 completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption' \u2014 none of which is revenue or retention. Shortening onboarding can lift completion by removing qualifying friction while degrading the quality of accounts that complete, so the archived record must show whether the lift persisted past week one and whether it converted to paid, retained revenue. (2) memory_73 is the obvious reflex given the competitor's entry pricing, and it is the single highest-risk inherited belief here: 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' is silent on retention, margin, and discount-cohort durability. Discount-acquired SMB accounts are exactly the cohort a competitor can re-poach, so matching price could book short-term revenue while destroying the long-term qualified base. I want that record before I let competitive pressure drive the slot. I did not spend budget on memory_57 (referral) because it already explicitly reports qualified revenue with no retention harm \u2014 it is the best-supported memory for this objective and needs verification least; nor on memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist), which is well-aligned to pipeline quality but does not address either declining metric this week. Current intent: simplify_onboarding, because it is the one lever that plausibly addresses both observed declines (onboarding completion -4% is upstream of activation -6%) rather than treating a symptom, and because it competes on product value rather than price. Standard experiment scale, not broad rollout: memory_86 and memory_31 are consolidated summaries whose underlying evidence I have not yet seen, memory_31 is from day 12 and may not describe today's funnel, and the earlier lifts were measured on activation-type metrics that are not the objective I am being judged on. If the archive shows memory_86's gain never propagated to retained revenue, or shows the completion lift came from dropping fields that were doing real qualification work, I will fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91, targets the larger -6% decline) or referral_incentive (memory_57, the only inherited belief already validated against qualified revenue). If memory_73 turns out to have durable retention evidence, promotional_pricing becomes defensible as a guarded test \u2014 but I will not commit to price-matching on an unverified acquisition-only result.

final.rationale: Both verifications paid off, and they resolve in opposite directions. exp_86 is stronger than the consolidated summary suggested: the +13% completion lift was accompanied by 30-day retention +3% and time-to-value -2.1 days. That is the specific check I wanted \u2014 the gain did not come from stripping out friction that was doing real qualification work, because the accounts that completed stayed. Completion, speed-to-value, and retention all moved the same way, which is the signature of a genuine value improvement rather than a proxy-metric artifact. exp_73 confirms the risk I flagged: the inherited summary ('strong acquisition and revenue lift') omitted 30-day retention -12%, and the original record explicitly warns against generalizing targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The +18% qualified revenue is a first-cycle number from a cohort that does not survive renewal. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, matching the competitor on price is the wrong move even though it is the most direct answer to the competitive pressure \u2014 it would book revenue this quarter and hand back the base next one. I am correcting memory_73 in place: it should be read as a warning, not a playbook. Final decision: simplify_onboarding. It is now the best-evidenced lever I have against the objective, it attacks the upstream cause (onboarding completion -4% feeding activation -6%) rather than a symptom, and it competes on delivered value rather than price \u2014 which is also the durable answer to a discount-led competitor, since accounts that reach value fast are the ones least worth re-poaching. Remaining uncertainty, held deliberately: exp_86's retention evidence stops at 30 days, so it demonstrates survival of the early window, not renewal-cycle durability \u2014 exactly the horizon where exp_73's cohort collapsed. The prior experiment also ran without a competitor actively pulling on this segment, so the effect size may not transfer intact. That is why I am running a standard experiment rather than a broad rollout: instrument to 30-day retention and first-renewal revenue, not to completion rate alone, so this run measures the thing the objective cares about instead of re-confirming the proxy. If the lift shows up in completion but not in retained revenue, that is a stop signal, and the fallback is activation_messaging (memory_91, addresses the larger -6% decline) or referral_incentive (memory_57, the only untouched belief already stated in qualified-revenue terms \u2014 though note it is a consolidated summary of the same kind that proved incomplete for memory_73, so it warrants verification before it drives a decision).
